overview.title: LinearModel as a torch.nn.Module, the SGD optimizer, and a simplified training step
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.subsection: 3.4.2 An end-to-end example: A linear classifier in pure PyTorch
overview.main_topic: Completing the LinearModel Module (Parameters W and b, forward()), calling it via __call__(), creating torch.optim.SGD from model.parameters(), and the three-call training step backward() / optimizer.step() / model.zero_grad()
overview.central_idea: Once W and b are torch.nn.Parameter attributes of a Module, the model can be called directly on inputs, its parameters can be handed to an optimizer with model.parameters(), and the manual no_grad update is replaced by optimizer.step() — so the training step shrinks to forward pass, loss, loss.backward(), optimizer.step(), model.zero_grad().
overview.importance: This is the idiomatic shape of PyTorch training code that the reader will meet everywhere, and the same Module/optimizer API underlies Keras models on the PyTorch backend (p.241).

summary:
The page finishes **Listing 3.27**. Inside `__init__()` (after `super().__init__()` on p.103) the model stores `self.W = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.rand(input_dim, output_dim))` and `self.b = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(output_dim))` — the same initial values as on p.102, but now wrapped as Parameters and held by the Module. `forward(self, inputs)` returns `torch.matmul(inputs, self.W) + self.b`.

The model is instantiated with `model = LinearModel()`. When using a `torch.nn.Module` instance you don't call `forward()` directly; you use `__call__()` — i.e., call the model object on the inputs — which redirects to `forward()` but adds a few framework hooks. The example converts the NumPy data first: `torch_inputs = torch.tensor(inputs)`, then `output = model(torch_inputs)`.

Next comes an optimizer. To instantiate one you must give it the list of parameters it should update, which a Module exposes through `.parameters()`: `optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)`.

With the Module and the SGD optimizer, the training step becomes `training_step(inputs, targets)`: `predictions = model(inputs)`, `loss = mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)`, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`, `model.zero_grad()`, `return loss`. W and b are no longer passed as arguments, because the model owns them.

The page then contrasts the old update — `with torch.no_grad(): W -= grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate; b -= grad_loss_wrt_b * learning_rate` — with the new one: "Now we can just do `optimizer.step()`." The matching explanation of `model.zero_grad()` (replacing the manual `.grad = None` resets) and the warning not to forget it are on p.105.

paragraphs.excerpt: We can now instantiate our LinearModel
paragraphs.what_it_says: After the class definition ends (the forward() method at the top of the page), the model is created with `model = LinearModel()`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instantiation runs `__init__()`: the Module base class is initialized and the two Parameters are created and registered — W with uniform random values of shape (2, 1), b with zeros of shape (1,). Note that `input_dim` and `output_dim` are read from the enclosing (global) scope defined on p.102, not passed to the constructor.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The name `model` now refers to an object rather than the function from p.102, which is why the simplified training step can call `model(inputs)` with a single argument.

paragraphs.excerpt: When using an instance of torch.nn.Module, rather than calling the forward() method
paragraphs.what_it_says: With a Module instance, you call the object itself on inputs (its `__call__()` method) rather than calling `forward()` directly; `__call__()` redirects to `forward()` but adds a few framework hooks. Example: `torch_inputs = torch.tensor(inputs)` and `output = model(torch_inputs)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: `model(x)` is the public entry point; `forward()` is where you write the computation. The hooks are extra behaviour the framework can run before or after forward (beyond the book: registered forward hooks, pre-hooks, and support used by tools such as torch.compile). The NumPy float32 `inputs` from p.94 must be turned into a torch tensor first.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Calling forward() directly would bypass those hooks and is considered a bug in PyTorch code. The same pattern exists in Keras, where you call a layer rather than its call() method (p.116).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: torch.tensor copies the NumPy data and keeps its dtype (float32 here); torch.from_numpy would share memory instead.

terminology.meaning: Python's special method invoked when an object is called like a function; Module.__call__ runs hooks and forward().
Extra code the framework runs around forward().

paragraphs.excerpt: Now, let's get our hands on a PyTorch optimizer. To instantiate it,
paragraphs.what_it_says: An optimizer must be given the list of parameters it will update; a Module provides it via `.parameters()`. Code: `optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: `model.parameters()` yields the registered Parameters — here W and b. The optimizer keeps references to them and, on each `step()`, applies its update rule using their `.grad`. With plain SGD and `lr=learning_rate` (0.1, defined on p.103) the rule is exactly the manual update from p.103.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is how the optimizer becomes 'aware' of the model, one of the hidden links the book calls 'spooky action at a distance' on p.105. Forgetting to pass the parameters (or passing the wrong ones) means nothing gets trained.

terminology.meaning: Module method returning an iterator over all Parameters registered on the module (and its submodules).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Using the Module and the SGD optimizer, the training step simplifies to: forward pass, loss, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`, `model.zero_grad()`, `return loss`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The step no longer takes W and b as arguments or touches them directly. `loss.backward()` still fills W.grad and b.grad; `optimizer.step()` performs the update; `model.zero_grad()` clears the gradients of all the model's parameters.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These three calls are the 'incantation' the book asks readers to memorize on p.105. The structure scales unchanged from this 3-parameter model to models with billions of parameters.

terminology.meaning: Applies one update to every parameter the optimizer manages, using their current .grad.
Resets the gradients of all of the module's parameters.

paragraphs.excerpt: Previously, updating the model parameters looked like this
paragraphs.what_it_says: The manual update from p.103 — two in-place subtractions inside `torch.no_grad()` — is shown again, followed by "Now we can just do `optimizer.step()`."
paragraphs.what_it_means: For SGD, `optimizer.step()` does precisely $p \leftarrow p - \eta\,\nabla_p\mathcal{L}$ for each parameter p, and does it without gradient tracking internally — so the `no_grad` block disappears from user code too.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Swapping in a different optimizer (e.g. `torch.optim.Adam`) changes the update rule without changing the training step, which is the main benefit of the abstraction (beyond the book).

concepts.name: torch.nn.Module
concepts.definition: PyTorch base class for models: Parameters are created in __init__(), the computation goes in forward(), and the instance is called directly on inputs.
concepts.intuition: A self-contained model object that owns its weights.
concepts.technical: LinearModel holds self.W (2, 1) and self.b (1,) as torch.nn.Parameter; forward returns torch.matmul(inputs, self.W) + self.b. model(x) goes through __call__, which runs hooks and then forward.
concepts.significance: Lets an optimizer find all trainable state via model.parameters() and lets model.zero_grad() reset everything at once.
concepts.misconception: That model.forward(x) and model(x) are interchangeable; only model(x) runs the framework hooks.

concepts.name: Optimizer (torch.optim.SGD)
concepts.definition: An object that holds a list of parameters and updates them from their gradients according to an update rule.
concepts.intuition: The part of training that 'takes the step' once the gradients are known.
concepts.technical: torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate); optimizer.step() performs p -= lr * p.grad for each parameter, replacing the manual no_grad update.
concepts.significance: Decouples the update rule from the training-step code.
concepts.misconception: That optimizer.step() also computes the gradients or clears them; backward() computes them and zero_grad() clears them.

concepts.name: Training step (Module + optimizer version)
concepts.definition: Forward pass, loss, loss.backward(), optimizer.step(), model.zero_grad().
concepts.technical: Each line maps to the manual version on p.103: backward() is unchanged, step() replaces the no_grad update, zero_grad() replaces .grad = None.
concepts.example: training_step(torch_inputs, torch_targets) returns the scalar loss.
concepts.misconception: That zero_grad() can be skipped because step() 'consumes' the gradients; it does not (p.105).

math.title: Update performed by optimizer.step() for plain SGD
math.latex: p \leftarrow p - \eta\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial p}\quad\text{for each } p \in \{W, b\},\qquad \eta = \texttt{learning\_rate}
math.source_text: with torch.no_grad(): W -= grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate; b -= grad_loss_wrt_b * learning_rate  →  optimizer.step()

variables.meaning: a parameter returned by model.parameters() (W or b)
lr passed to torch.optim.SGD (learning_rate = 0.1 from p.103)

math.operations: Gradient-scaled in-place subtraction for every managed parameter.
math.purpose: Shows that optimizer.step() is the same update the page shows being replaced.
math.interpretation: The optimizer generalizes the two hand-written lines to any number of parameters.
math.intuition: One downhill step for every weight at once.

code.title: The simplified training step
code.original_code:
def training_step(inputs, targets):
    predictions = model(inputs)
    loss = mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    model.zero_grad()
    return loss
code.what_it_does: One gradient-descent step using the Module and optimizer.

line_explanations.explanation: W and b are no longer arguments; the model owns them.
Forward pass via __call__ and the MSE loss from p.102.

pitfalls: Forgetting model.zero_grad() is a major and common bug (p.105).

deeper.title: Manual vs Module/optimizer step, side by side
deeper.body:
| Manual (p.103) | Module + optimizer (p.104) |
|---|---|
| `training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)` | `training_step(inputs, targets)` |
| `model(inputs, W, b)` (function) | `model(inputs)` (Module `__call__`) |
| `loss.backward()` | `loss.backward()` |
| `W.grad, b.grad` read by hand | read internally by the optimizer |
| `with torch.no_grad(): W -= ...; b -= ...` | `optimizer.step()` |
| `W.grad = None; b.grad = None` | `model.zero_grad()` |

`loss.backward()` is the only line that is identical — gradient computation does not change; only bookkeeping is automated.

deeper.title: How the three objects find each other
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, a look at the 'spooky action at a distance' mentioned on p.105:
1. `torch.nn.Parameter` assignments in `__init__` are registered by `Module.__setattr__`, so `model.parameters()` can list W and b.
2. The optimizer stores those same tensor objects (not copies).
3. The forward pass uses those tensors, so the loss graph leads back to them.
4. `loss.backward()` writes gradients onto the very tensors the optimizer holds; `optimizer.step()` reads `p.grad` from them; `model.zero_grad()` clears `p.grad` on the same objects.
Nothing is passed explicitly because all three share references to W and b.

takeaways: A Module stores Parameters in __init__() (self.W, self.b) and computes in forward().
Call the module itself, model(x); __call__() runs hooks and then forward().
An optimizer is built from model.parameters() and a learning rate: torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate).
The training step reduces to loss.backward(), optimizer.step(), model.zero_grad().
optimizer.step() replaces the manual no_grad update; loss.backward() is unchanged.

questions.question: Could you rewrite LinearModel so input_dim and output_dim are constructor arguments, and still train it with the same training step?
questions.answer: Yes: def __init__(self, input_dim, output_dim): super().__init__(); self.W = ...; self.b = ...; then model = LinearModel(2, 1). The training step is unchanged.
